content:
It's nice that we have the new declarations diff which reliably reports the new/removed declarations by name. It would be nice to have the same for declaration bodies as well, even just at the level of saying a new PR doesn't change any declaration at all.

We sometimes have large refactor PRs which should theoretically do nothing, e.g. they are fixing some technical debt by modifying proofs but no statements should change. It would be nice for reviewing them if we could also report that a PR changes no declaration bodies either. In particular I'm inspired by a PR that changes many instances of the use of classical reasoning across mathlib, including in some definition where it could also change which decidability instance is chosen in a _definition_ that could then have subtle downstream effects. Reviewing large refactor PRs is difficult and it occurred to me that this would be a nice tool to have. Even for ordinary PRs it would be nice to know if an innocent change accidentally changed the type of something.

I imagine this might already be easily available by figuring out some deterministic hashing scheme on top of what lean already exports, but I'm not familiar with the available interfaces or whether it's been tried before--a zulip search didn't give me anything relevant. Has anyone tried this before?
Sounds like an use case for Ix (cc @John Burnham)
There is a semantic diffing tool in the works (not by me). Info coming soon I believe

There is @Adam Topaz 's https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/semantic_hash which is related. @Damiano Testa also has some ideas in this direction too, and I'm hoping to start working on related tooling in the coming weeks.

Two related feature requests:

  • ensure that declarations' pretty-printed output stays the same before and after
  • a variant: ensure that declarations are the same before and after modulo naming universe variables

(There are refactoring PRs of the kind "name this free universe variable", and they are a nightmare to review without proper tooling. Though of course I could hack something together, if I know which declarations changed.)

#mathlib4 > Declarations diff in Lean @ 💬
Also Leaff https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VkKfIWoM3Ms, and Jovan Gerbscheid's #33640 does some type normalization for decls (for a different purpose but slightly similar) which might be useful.

Bryan Gin-ge Chen said:

There is Adam Topaz 's https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/semantic_hash which is related.

Very cool! This approach is lighter than what we do for Ix, but about 10x more performant (7.8s vs 85s). Some differences:

  1. The big difference is that Ix doesn't use hash-consing, but rather serializes Lean into a compact binary format called Ixon (docs: https://github.com/argumentcomputer/ix/blob/main/docs/Ixon.md), which we then hash directly. Mathlib, for example, hashes to about 450mb in anonymous mode, and 3GB with metadata included (allowing for lossless decompilation back to the Lean4 kernel).
  2. Ix uses cryptographic 256-bit Blake3 hashing instead of the mixHash UInt64 digests to avoid collisions. The latter is probably fine for just the semantic diff use case. We have to use blake3 though, because we have to account for a malicious adversary forcing a collision, which would break Ix's zero-knowledge proofs of Lean4 typechecking.
  3. I think Ix separates out non-semantic metadata a bit more thoroughly, such as BinderInfo and ReducibilityHints. Some of that is needed in practice for typechecking performance, but we treat this as non-deterministic hints to our prover.
  4. Ix is a bit more invasive regarding its anonymous content addressing. We wanted to canonicalize mutual blocks in a minimal and order invariant way rather than just taking the Lean4 source order like semantic_hash does. In Ix, for example, the following two mutual blocks produce constants with the same hashes
namespace AuxDedup1

mutual
  inductive A : Type where | mk : List B → List C → A
  inductive B : Type where | leaf : B
  inductive C : Type where | leaf : C
end

end AuxDedup1

namespace AuxDedup2

  inductive C : Type where | leaf : C
mutual
  inductive A : Type where | mk : List B → List C → A
  inductive B : Type where | leaf : B
end

This, however, requires reimplementing the generation of auxiliary constants like .rec_N or .below, which can encode the source order in their semantic structure, such as motive arguments. In effect, we have to do redo a small part of the elaboration step, which is aggressive, but it significantly helps reduce pressure on our zero-knowledge prover because more constants can structurally merge.

Overall, I think the two tools are very similar, but not identical functionally due to some of the above differences. I've just made a PR for an ix diff tool (https://github.com/argumentcomputer/ix/pull/474) that exposes more of the functionality directly. We'll likely merge this in the next few days, but might be of interest now if people want to experiment with it. I've attached a transcript of what the tool returns for mathlib on rev = "4.29" with commit 8850ed93.

@John Burnham — thanks for the interest in the semantic hash package! Indeed the my main focus was to make it as fast as possible since it was originally intended for semantic diffing applications. ix sounds quite interesting! I’ll have to take a closer look soon.
